---
title: "Undirected GGMs from single-cell transcriptomics"
---

DeCovarT needs **one sparse Gaussian graphical model per cell type at
the population (pseudo-bulk) level**, not a per-cell precision and not a
directed regulatory DAG. The estimand, aligned with the article, is

$$
\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot j}
\sim
\mathcal{N}_{G}\bigl(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}\bigr),
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{j}
\equiv
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{-1}
\ \text{sparse},
$$ {#eq-grn-estimand}

with undirected edges encoding conditional dependence
[@friedmanSparseInverseCovariance2008; @mazumderGraphicalLassoNew2011].
We write $\boldsymbol{\Omega}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}$ for the precision
and keep $\theta$ for a generic parameter, not for a precision entry.
Hats, checks and asterisks distinguish estimators from the truth:

- $\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{\ast}$ (entries $\omega_{gg'}^{\ast}$) is the
  **true** precision;
- $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$ is the **sparse** $\ell_{1}$ estimator
  (graphical lasso or penalised PLN);
- $\check{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$ is the **de-sparsified** matrix obtained
  by one Newton step from $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$. Use the caron
  only when the two matrices could be confused: $\check{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$
  is dense and intended for entrywise inference, not as the DeCovarT
  plug-in.

The object exported to the convolution is the sparse SPD matrix
$\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{j}$ (or an SPD refit on an FDR support),
on the linear scale of @eq-grn-convolution.

Single-cell UMI profiles are the **only observations**.
They are **not** the objects that enter the deconvolution likelihood: we use them to
**estimate** $(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{j})$ for labelled
types in the Suppinger murine gastruloid resource
[@suppingerMultimodalCharacterizationMurine2023]. Downstream, those
parameters discriminate types via mean shifts **and** precision rewiring,
then enter the convolution

$$
\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}
\mid
(\boldsymbol{\zeta},\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})
\sim
\mathcal{N}_{G}\!\bigl(
\boldsymbol{\mu}\,\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i},\,
\textstyle\sum_{j}p_{ji}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}
\bigr).
$$ {#eq-grn-convolution}

## Scope of the core pipeline {#sec-grn-scope}

**In scope:** undirected sparse precisions and dense covariances;
single-cell transcriptomics only; stationarity; labelled cell types.
@fig-grn-core shows five strategies:

- the `ppcor` baseline (@sec-ppcor);
- the graphical lasso, fitted with `glasso` (@sec-huge);
- `SILGGM` after a nonparanormal map, with global FDR (@sec-silggm);
- `PLNnetwork` (@sec-pln);
- a dense shrinkage covariance (@sec-shrinkage).

**Dataset constraint.** GSE229513 is a 10x Chromium 3′ v3 UMI resource
with **one** technical scRNA-seq experiment, not independent biological
replicates for GRNs
[@suppingerMultimodalCharacterizationMurine2023]. GSE250136 is a later
stem-embryo dataset; it is external validation, not extra Suppinger
replicates. Technical bootstrap of cells is allowed
(@sec-align-bootstrap); biological bootstrap is not. Networks are fit
independently at 48 h, 72 h and 96 h (@sec-geo-design).

## How each estimator sees the counts {#sec-grn-observation}

A transformation belongs to **one** estimator. It is not crossed with
the other two.

| Estimator | What is passed in | Object exported |
|-----------|-------------------|-----------------|
| `ppcor` | Continuous Gaussian table, $n>p$ | SPD refit on the BH support |
| `glasso` | Correlation matrix of a continuous table | Sparse $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{j}$, rescaled |
| `SILGGM` | Nonparanormal scores, then global FDR | Support, then an SPD refit |
| `PLNnetwork` | Raw UMI counts and a library-size offset | Latent Gaussian precision |
| `corpcor` shrinkage | Continuous Gaussian table | Dense $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}$ |

`SCTransform` Pearson residuals stay in the HVG ranking of
@sec-fs-hvg. Do not pass them to `PLNnetwork`: the PLN already has a
Poisson sampling layer. The nonparanormal map is part of the `SILGGM`
branch only (@nte-npn-derivation).


## Five covariance and precision estimators {#sec-grn-core}

### Baseline: partial correlations by inversion (`ppcor`) {#sec-ppcor}

Before any penalty, invert the sample covariance and read the partial
correlations off the precision. This is the baseline that every
penalised estimator should beat. `ppcor` computes
$\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}=S^{-1}$, the partial correlations of
@eq-partial, and a $t$ test per pair,
$t=\hat\rho\sqrt{(n-2-k)/(1-\hat\rho^{2})}$ with $k=p-2$ controlled
genes [@R-ppcor].
Benjamini–Hochberg on the $p(p-1)/2$ tests gives a support $\hat E$.

Going back from $\hat\rho$ to a precision on the scale of the data
needs **conditional**, not marginal, variances:

$$
\omega_{gg}=\frac{1}{\operatorname{Var}(x_{g}\mid
\boldsymbol{x}_{-g})},
\qquad
\omega_{gg'}=-\rho_{gg'\mid\mathrm{rest}}\sqrt{\omega_{gg}\,\omega_{g'g'}}.
$$ {#eq-ppcor-rescale}

Rescaling by the marginal variances $s_{gg}$ understates each
$\omega_{gg}$ by the factor $1-R^{2}_{g\cdot\mathrm{rest}}$. Once the
non-significant $\hat\rho$ are set to zero, the matrix is no longer
guaranteed to be positive definite. Refit an SPD precision under the
zeros of $\hat E$ instead (@eq-hard-cov-selection-repro below). This is
Dempster's covariance selection, which exists when $n$ exceeds the
maximum-likelihood threshold of the selected graph.

The baseline is limited to $n>p$. With $p\ge n$, `ppcor` falls back to
the Moore–Penrose inverse and returns no test. At $p=500$ panel genes it
applies only to the largest types, or to a sub-panel. For $p\ge n$ the
closest unpenalised analogue is the shrinkage estimator of
@sec-shrinkage [@schäferShrinkageApproachLargescale2005], with a local
FDR on its partial correlations. It shrinks towards the diagonal, so it
shares part of the attenuation discussed in the DeCovarT network
vignette.

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{\hat E}
=
\arg\max_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}\succ0}
\log\det\boldsymbol{\Omega}-\operatorname{tr}(S\boldsymbol{\Omega})
\quad\text{s.t.}\quad
\omega_{gg'}=0\ \ \forall\,(g,g')\notin\hat E .
$$ {#eq-hard-cov-selection-repro}

### Graphical lasso with an unpenalised diagonal (`glasso`) {#sec-huge}

The programme is the graphical lasso of Friedman, Hastie and Tibshirani
[@friedmanSparseInverseCovariance2008; @mazumderGraphicalLassoNew2011].
`scripts/03_01_grn_huge.R` keeps its historical name. It now calls
`glasso::glasso()` [@R-glasso] instead of `huge` [@zhaoHugePackageHighdimensional; @R-huge],
because `huge.glasso()` always penalises the diagonal (see below). The
penalty is chosen by the EBIC path of @sec-huge-lambda.

#### Generative model

Cells of one labelled type, at one time, are treated as independent
Gaussian replicates. The precision is sparse.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-huge-gen
%%| fig-cap: "Graphical lasso generative model: independent Gaussian cells of one type, with a sparse precision."
%%{init: {"theme": "sandstone", "flowchart": {"curve": "basis"}}}%%
flowchart TB
  subgraph plateC["c = 1, ..., n_j"]
    direction TB
    mu["mu_j"] --> x(("x_c"))
    Sig["Sigma_j"] --> x
  end
  Th["Omega_j = Sigma_j inverse, sparse"] --> Sig
  classDef param fill:#ffffff,stroke:#0f172a,stroke-width:1.5px
  classDef latent fill:#ffffff,stroke:#0f172a,stroke-width:1.5px
  class mu,Sig,Th param
  class x latent
```

#### Objective and assumptions

Let $S$ be the sample covariance of the $n$ cells on the gene panel,
$D=\operatorname{diag}(S)$, and $R=D^{-1/2}SD^{-1/2}$ the sample
correlation. The estimator penalises the off-diagonal entries only:

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{R}
=
\arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}\succ 0}
\Bigl[
-\log\det\boldsymbol{\Omega}
+
\operatorname{tr}(R\boldsymbol{\Omega})
+
\lambda\sum_{g\neq g'}|\omega_{gg'}|
\Bigr],
\qquad
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}
=
D^{-1/2}\,\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{R}\,D^{-1/2}.
$$ {#eq-glasso}

Working on $R$ puts every gene on the same scale for one $\lambda$, as a
common penalty requires. Rescaling leaves the zeros and the partial
correlations unchanged.

Assumptions: multivariate Gaussian observations; conditional
independence encoded by zeros of $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$; cells independent
within the type-time subset; $G$ may exceed $n$.

#### Optimisation and the $\ell_{1}$ penalty

`glasso::glasso(R, rho = lambda, penalize.diagonal = FALSE)` solves
@eq-glasso by block coordinate descent. The $\ell_{1}$ term drives
off-diagonal entries to zero. **`penalize.diagonal` defaults to `TRUE`
in `glasso` 1.11**, so it must be set explicitly. With `FALSE`, the
fitted covariance $W=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{R}^{-1}$ keeps
$W_{gg}=R_{gg}=1$. Once rescaled, $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}$
therefore matches the sample variances.

The switch from `huge` follows from two facts, checked in the `huge`
1.5.1 sources (`huge.glasso()` and `src/huge_core.cpp`):

- **The data are standardised.** Given a data matrix, `huge.glasso()`
  runs `scale(x)` and works on $R=\operatorname{cor}(x)$. `icov` is the
  precision of the standardised genes. On the scale of $x$ it is
  $D^{-1/2}\,\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{R}\,D^{-1/2}$, with
  $D=\operatorname{diag}(S)$.
- **The diagonal is penalised.** The solver sets
  $W_{gg}=R_{gg}+\lambda=1+\lambda$ for $W=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}^{-1}$,
  so an isolated gene has precision $1/(1+\lambda)$. `cov.output = TRUE`
  returns this $W$, the dual of the same fit: $W_{gg'}=R_{gg'}+\lambda\,
  \mathrm{sign}(\hat\omega_{gg'})$ on the edges and
  $|W_{gg'}-R_{gg'}|\le\lambda$ elsewhere. It is not a separate
  covariance refit on the support. `huge.glasso()` has no switch for
  the diagonal; `glasso::glasso(penalize.diagonal = FALSE)` is the
  unpenalised alternative.

Three behaviours of the earlier script are corrected:

1. **Scale.** The $\lambda$ endpoints and the EBIC log-likelihood were
   computed from $S$, while `huge` fitted $R$. All three now use $R$.
   The exported $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$ and
   $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}$ are rescaled to the data
   (`rescale_correlation_fit()`).
2. **Constant genes.** One gene constant across the cells of a type used
   to return a diagonal covariance for all 500 genes. That gene is now
   left out of the type's graph and recorded in `excluded_genes`.
   Pairwise Hellinger and overlap scores use the genes both types keep.
3. **Failed solves.** A failed penalty used to be replaced by a diagonal
   precision, which EBIC could then select. It is now dropped from the
   path and listed in `failed_lambda`.

#### Hyperparameters

- $\lambda$ path and EBIC $\gamma$ (`ebic_adaptive_path()`,
  [@foygelExtendedBayesianInformation2010]); StARS
  [@liuStabilityApproachRegularization2010] as a diagnostic only;
- `penalize.diagonal = FALSE`, on the correlation scale;
- the gene panel $\mathcal{G}_{0}$ and the type-time subset.

#### Choosing $\lambda$ {#sec-huge-lambda}

All three core estimators share the same **endpoints**, then branch on
what the path is for.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-lambda-strategies
%%| fig-cap: "Penalty-path strategies. The endpoints are shared. Only the safeguarded EBIC interval search is implemented; TAV and global-local shrinkage remain alternatives."
%%{init: {"theme": "sandstone"}}%%
flowchart TD
  S["Sample correlation R"] --> Lmax["lambda_max = max off-diagonal |R_ij|"]
  N["n cells, p genes"] --> Lmin["lambda_min of order C sqrt(log p / n)"]
  Lmax --> Branch{"Objective"}
  Lmin --> Branch
  Branch -->|"minimise EBIC"| EBIC["Safeguarded log-interval search"]
  Branch -->|"recover the support"| TAV["TAV / thAV, one line search"]
  Branch -->|"no global lambda"| HS["Graphical horseshoe / spike-and-slab"]
  EBIC --> Fit["At most 40 precision solves"]
```

1. **Shared endpoints.** At
   $\lambda_{\max}=\max_{g\neq g'}|R_{gg'}|$ the off-diagonal precision
   is zero. Useful regularisation sits at order
   $\lambda_{\min}\asymp C\sqrt{\log p/n}$, so the search does not
   waste solves near the unregularised MLE.
2. **EBIC interval search (implemented).** The target is
   $\lambda^{\star}=\arg\min_{\lambda}\mathrm{EBIC}_{\gamma}(\lambda)$
   [@foygelExtendedBayesianInformation2010]. Six log-spaced anchors,
   then geometric midpoints
   $\sqrt{\lambda_{L}\lambda_{R}}$ in the basin of the current minimum,
   while neighbouring intervals stay alive. That is **not** golden
   section: EBIC jumps when an edge appears or disappears, so a
   unimodal search would be the wrong algorithm. The same driver,
   `ebic_adaptive_path()`, takes a `fit_precision` callback, so
   `SILGGM` and `PLNnetwork` can reuse it.
3. **TAV, if the target is the support.** Thresholded adaptive
   validation
   [@laszkiewiczThresholdedAdaptiveValidation2021]
   calibrates graphical lasso for **graph recovery** with at most one
   line search. We document it here and do not implement it in the core
   scripts.
4. **Global-local shrinkage, if there should be no $\lambda$ path.** A
   graphical horseshoe [@liGraphicalHorseshoeEstimator2019] puts a
   half-Cauchy local scale on each $\omega_{gg'}$ and a global scale
   $\tau$. That replaces the lasso path rather than choosing 40 lasso
   penalties, and it is heavier than the EBIC search.

::: {#nte-stars-cost .callout-warning}
## :warning: Why we do not run StARS on this panel

StARS asks whether edges are stable under subsampling
[@liuStabilityApproachRegularization2010]. The cost is $B\times L$
graphical-lasso fits. In `huge.select()` the default is 20 subsamples,
and for $n>144$ each subsample has size $10\sqrt{n}$. At $n=5{,}000$
that is about 700 cells per subsample; 20 penalties then become on
the order of 400 full-data-scale solves, not 40. We keep StARS as a
stability **diagnostic** in @sec-metrics-stat, not as the selector for
$\mathcal{G}_{0}=500$.
:::

### `SILGGM` after a nonparanormal map {#sec-silggm}

`SILGGM` tests entries of a Gaussian precision and controls FDR on the
whole graph [@zhangSILGGMExtensivePackage2018; @R-SILGGM]. The arm used
here is: nonparanormal scores, then de-sparsified graphical lasso
(`D-S_GL`) with `global = TRUE`. With many cells the five `SILGGM`
procedures tend to agree; at a bulk-sample size they need not. The
object we keep is the **SPD precision refit on the FDR support**, not
the dense de-sparsified matrix.

::: {#nte-npn-derivation .callout-note}
## :information_source: Shrinkage versus truncation in `huge.npn`

Liu, Lafferty and Wasserman
[@liuNonparanormalSemiparametricEstimation2009] define a nonparanormal
vector by monotone maps $f_{g}$ such that
$Z_{g}=f_{g}(X_{g})$ and
$\boldsymbol{Z}\sim\mathcal{N}_{G}(\boldsymbol{0},R)$, with latent precision
$\boldsymbol{\Omega}=R^{-1}$. By Sklar's theorem, if the margins $F_{g}$
are continuous,

$$
F_{\boldsymbol{X}}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{G})
=
C_{R}\bigl(F_{1}(x_{1}),\ldots,F_{G}(x_{G})\bigr),
$$

where $C_{R}$ is the Gaussian copula with correlation $R$. Then
$U_{g}=F_{g}(X_{g})\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)$ and

$$
Z_{g}
=
\Phi^{-1}\bigl(F_{g}(X_{g})\bigr).
$$

The unknown monotone margins change the observed scale, not the latent
copula graph.

Let $R_{ig}=\operatorname{rank}(X_{ig})$ in a sample of size $n$. The
raw empirical cdf $\widehat{F}_{g}(X_{ig})=R_{ig}/n$ hits $1$ at the
sample maximum, and $\Phi^{-1}(1)=+\infty$. The score map is also
unstable in the tails because

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}u}\Phi^{-1}(u)
=
\frac{1}{\phi\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(u)\bigr)}
$$

diverges as $u\downarrow 0$ or $u\uparrow 1$. `huge.npn()` therefore
regularises the plotting positions before $\Phi^{-1}$
[@R-huge]. Both options address that instability; truncation is not
intrinsically a “heavy-tail model”.

**Shrinkage** (`npn.func = "shrinkage"`, the `huge` default, and ours)
uses the plotting positions $R_{ig}/(n+1)$:

$$
\widetilde{Z}_{ig}^{\mathrm{shr}}
=
\Phi^{-1}\!\left(\frac{R_{ig}}{n+1}\right).
$$

Attainable probabilities lie in
$\{1/(n+1),\ldots,n/(n+1)\}$, so every Gaussian score stays finite
and each distinct rank keeps a distinct score. Relative to $R_{ig}/n$
the shift is at most $1/(n+1)$, not an $O(n^{-1/2})$ pull toward
$1/2$.

**Truncation** (`npn.func = "truncation"`) winsorises $R_{ig}/n$ at
$\delta_{n}$ before $\Phi^{-1}$. Unless `npn.thresh` is set, `huge`
uses

$$
\delta_{n}
=
\frac{1}{4\,n^{1/4}\sqrt{\pi\log n}}
=
O\bigl(n^{-1/4}(\log n)^{-1/2}\bigr),
$$

not order $n^{-1/2}$. Central ranks are unchanged; all probabilities
beyond the cutoff share the same endpoint score
$\Phi^{-1}(\delta_{n})$ or $\Phi^{-1}(1-\delta_{n})$. That clips the
tails more aggressively and discards rank information past the cutoff.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{shrinkage:}
&\quad
\widetilde{Z}_{ig}
=
\Phi^{-1}\!\left(\frac{R_{ig}}{n+1}\right),
\\
\text{truncation:}
&\quad
\widetilde{Z}_{ig}
=
\Phi^{-1}\!\left[
\min\bigl\{1-\delta_{n},\,
\max(\delta_{n},R_{ig}/n)\bigr\}
\right].
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-npn-shrink-trunc}

`huge.npn()` then standardises columns. The output of `shrinkage` or
`truncation` is an $n\times G$ score matrix (`skeptic` returns a
correlation matrix instead). Graphical lasso on those scores targets
$\boldsymbol{\Omega}=R^{-1}$ of the latent Gaussian $\boldsymbol{Z}$, not the
precision of the raw counts. Means on this scale are not
$\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}$.

![Two regularisations of $\Phi^{-1}$ in `huge.npn()`: truncation clips
the empirical tails at $\delta_{n}$; shrinkage moves the whole rank
grid strictly inside $(0,1)$. Both keep Gaussian scores finite before
the latent graph is estimated.](images/npn_shrinkage_truncation.png){#fig-npn-shrink-trunc}
:::

#### Generative model

Observed margins are monotone images of one latent Gaussian vector.
The precision that `SILGGM` tests is the precision of that latent
vector, not of the counts.

```{mermaid}

%%| label: fig-silggm-gen
%%| fig-cap: "Nonparanormal generative model: each gene margin is a monotone map of a latent Gaussian coordinate. SILGGM tests the precision of that latent vector."
%%{init: {"theme": "sandstone", "flowchart": {"curve": "basis"}}}%%
flowchart TB
  subgraph plateC["c = 1, ..., n_j"]
    direction TB
    R["Correlation R"] --> Z(("Z_c"))
    Z --> f["Monotone f_g"]
    f --> X(["X_c"])
  end
  Th["Precision of Z, sparse"] --> R
  classDef param fill:#ffffff,stroke:#0f172a,stroke-width:1.5px
  classDef latent fill:#ffffff,stroke:#0f172a,stroke-width:1.5px
  classDef obs fill:#cbd5e1,stroke:#0f172a,stroke-width:1.5px
  class R,Th,f param
  class Z latent
  class X obs
```

#### Objective and the de-sparsified correction

The first step is still @eq-glasso, which is $\ell_{1}$-biased. The
Janková–van de Geer correction
[@jankovaConfidenceIntervalsHighdimensional2015] is **not**
$2\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}-S$. On the correlation scale it is the
one-step Newton update

$$
\check{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}
=
2\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}
-
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}\,
\widehat{R}\,
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}},
$$ {#eq-desparsify}

with $\widehat{R}$ the empirical correlation of the NPN scores (replace
$\widehat{R}$ by $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}$ on the covariance
scale). $\check{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$ recentres the edges so that they are
asymptotically normal under a sparsity condition on the maximum
degree. It is deliberately **dense**: it is an inferential object, not
a generative precision. Zhang and Zou
[@zhangSparsePrecisionMatrix2014] note that graphical lasso remains
useful for **support** recovery even when the Gaussian assumption
fails. That supports edge screening, not export of
$\check{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$ itself as $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{j}$.

::: {#nte-desparsify .callout-note}
## :information_source: One Newton step removes the first-order $\ell_{1}$ bias

The graphical-lasso KKT condition at $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$ is

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}
-
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}^{-1}
+
\lambda\widehat{\boldsymbol{Z}}
=
0,
$$

where $\widehat{Z}_{gg'}\in[-1,1]$ is a subgradient of the $\ell_{1}$
norm (and $\widehat{Z}_{gg'}=\operatorname{sign}(\hat\omega_{gg'})$
when $\hat\omega_{gg'}\neq 0$). The penalised estimator therefore does
**not** solve the unpenalised score
$g(\boldsymbol{\Omega})=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}-\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}=0$.
The leftover score $\lambda\widehat{\boldsymbol{Z}}$ **is** the
first-order shrinkage bias.

The Fréchet derivative of $g$ at $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$ maps
$H\mapsto\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}H\boldsymbol{\Omega}^{-1}$, so its inverse
sends $A\mapsto\boldsymbol{\Omega}A\boldsymbol{\Omega}$. One Newton step from
$\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$ is therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}
\check{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}
&=
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}
-
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}
\bigl(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}^{-1}\bigr)
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}
\\
&=
2\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}
-
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}\,
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\,
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}},
\end{aligned}
$$

which is @eq-desparsify on the covariance scale. Equivalently,
$\check{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}+\lambda\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}\widehat{\boldsymbol{Z}}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$:
the correction adds back the KKT bias term.

Under the usual sparsity and rate conditions the remainder after this
linear expansion is $o_{p}(n^{-1/2})$, so a **single** Newton step is
enough for entrywise $\sqrt{n}$-normality
[@jankovaConfidenceIntervalsHighdimensional2015]:

$$
\sqrt{n}\,
(\check\omega_{gg'}-\omega_{gg'}^{\ast})
\;\xrightarrow{d}\;
\mathcal{N}\bigl(0,\;
\omega_{gg}^{\ast}\omega_{g'g'}^{\ast}
+(\omega_{gg'}^{\ast})^{2}
\bigr).
$$

The plug-in standard error is
$\widehat{\mathrm{se}}(\check\omega_{gg'})
=\sqrt{(\hat\omega_{gg}\hat\omega_{g'g'}+\hat\omega_{gg'}^{2})/n}$.
`SILGGM` (`D-S_GL`, `global = TRUE`) thresholds these de-sparsified
$z$-statistics by the Liu–et-al.\ global FDR rule at
$\alpha=0.05$
[@liuGaussianGraphicalModel2013]. The resulting **support** is sparse;
$\check{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$ itself stays dense. DeCovarT then refits an
SPD $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{j}$ on that support.

![One Newton step de-sparsifies the graphical lasso: the $\ell_{1}$
estimator $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$ is biased and sparse; the
corrected $\check{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$ is dense and asymptotically
normal entrywise, which is what the FDR threshold uses.](images/desparsified_graphical_lasso.png){#fig-desparsify}
:::

#### Optimisation and global FDR

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-silggm-steps
%%| fig-cap: "Estimation order for the SILGGM arm: nonparanormal scores, graphical lasso, de-sparsified matrix, global FDR support, then an SPD refit. The debiased matrix is not exported."
%%{init: {"theme": "sandstone"}}%%
flowchart LR
  X["Counts"] --> N["Nonparanormal scores"]
  N --> Gl["Graphical lasso"]
  Gl --> T["Debiased check-Omega"]
  T --> FDR["Global FDR support"]
  FDR --> SPD["SPD refit"]
```

`SILGGM` runs a lasso-type fit, builds the debiased statistics, and,
with `global = TRUE`, thresholds them by the global FDR rule for
Gaussian graphical models
[@liuGaussianGraphicalModel2013; @zhangSILGGMExtensivePackage2018].
The selected
zeros define a support. An SPD precision is then refit on that support
(graphical lasso constrained to the support, or a small ridge if the
constrained MLE is unavailable). Edge testing and the DeCovarT precision
stay separate (@eq-grn-estimand).

#### Hyperparameters

- `npn.func`: `shrinkage` (default) or `truncation` (@nte-npn-derivation);
- `method = "D-S_GL"` and `global = TRUE`;
- FDR level $\alpha=0.05$;
- `lambda` if it is not left at the package default.

### Poisson-lognormal network {#sec-pln}

`PLNnetwork` is the sparse-precision member of `PLNmodels`
[@chiquetPoissonLognormalModelVersatile2021;
@chiquetVariationalInferenceSparse2018; @R-PLNmodels]. Fused PLN
graphical lasso is a perspective (@sec-grn-appendix), not this arm.

#### Generative model

For each cell $c$ in one type-time subset, with library size $S_{c}$,

$$
Y_{cg}\mid\boldsymbol{Z}_{c}
\sim
\mathrm{Poisson}(S_{c}Z_{cg}),
\qquad
\log\boldsymbol{Z}_{c}
\sim
\mathcal{N}_{G}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}),
\quad
\boldsymbol{\Omega}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}.
$$ {#eq-pln}

Zeros are Poisson sampling zeros
[@svenssonDropletScRNAseqNot2020]. The fit is **independent** for each
labelled type at each of 48 h, 72 h and 96 h. A single formula with
cell-type and time dummies would estimate **one** shared precision and
only shift the mean; that is not the DeCovarT target. The formula
interface is used inside each subset, with an offset and no further
design.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-pln-gen
%%| fig-cap: "PLNnetwork: library size offsets a Poisson mean whose log-intensity is a sparse Gaussian. One such model per type and time."
%%{init: {"theme": "sandstone", "flowchart": {"curve": "basis"}}}%%
flowchart TB
  subgraph plateC["c in one type-time subset"]
    direction TB
    S["offset log S_c"] --> Y(["Y_c"])
    Z(("log Z_c")) --> Y
    mu["mu"] --> Z
    Sig["Sigma"] --> Z
  end
  Th["Omega = Sigma inverse, sparse"] --> Sig
  classDef param fill:#ffffff,stroke:#0f172a,stroke-width:1.5px
  classDef latent fill:#ffffff,stroke:#0f172a,stroke-width:1.5px
  classDef obs fill:#cbd5e1,stroke:#0f172a,stroke-width:1.5px
  class mu,Sig,Th,S param
  class Z latent
  class Y obs
```

#### Objective and assumptions

The observed-data likelihood integrates the latent Gaussian. That
integral is intractable. Variational inference replaces the posterior
of $\boldsymbol{Z}$ by a tractable $q$ and maximises the evidence lower
bound, which is the expected complete log-likelihood minus
$\mathrm{KL}(q\,\|\,p(Z\mid Y))$. An $\ell_{1}$ penalty is added on
off-diagonal entries of $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$.

::: {#nte-vi-em .callout-important}
## :information_source: Variational EM, KL, and why not Monte Carlo

EM alternates an expectation under the **true** conditional
$p(Z\mid Y)$ with a maximisation of the expected complete
log-likelihood. When that conditional is unavailable, variational EM
restricts the expectation to a family $q$. The identity

$$
\log p(Y)
=
\mathrm{ELBO}(q)
+
\mathrm{KL}\bigl(q\,\|\,p(Z\mid Y)\bigr)
$$

shows that maximising the ELBO is the same as minimising the
Kullback–Leibler divergence from $q$ to the true posterior. Equality
holds when $q=p(Z\mid Y)$, which is ordinary EM. A Monte Carlo E-step
would draw the latent Gaussian at every iteration. The variational step
replaces those draws by a closed-form update of $q$, which is why the
same sparse PLN is practical at single-cell $n$
[@chiquetVariationalInferenceSparse2018].
:::

#### Optimisation and the $\ell_{1}$ penalty

`PLNnetwork()` runs that variational scheme over a grid of penalties
([PLNnetwork](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/PLNmodels/versions/0.10.6/topics/PLNnetwork)).
The pair-specific graphical-lasso weight is $\rho_{gg'}=\lambda w_{gg'}$.
`penalize_diagonal` stays `FALSE` in `control_main`, matching the
graphical-lasso convention. The penalty grid is set by `penalties`, or
by `nPenalties` and `min.ratio` in `control_init`.

The inner continuous problem in $(B,M,S)$ at fixed $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$
is solved by NLopt. We keep the conservative quadratic solver
**`CCSAQ`** as the default `algorithm`
[@chiquetVariationalInferenceSparse2018].

```pseudocode
#| label: algo-plnnetwork
#| html-line-number: true
#| pdf-line-number: true

\begin{algorithm}
\caption{PLNnetwork alternating variational / graphical-lasso optimisation}
\begin{algorithmic}
\Require Counts $Y$, covariates $X$, offsets $O$, penalty $\lambda$
\Require penalty weights $W$
\Require inner tolerances $(f_{\mathrm{rel}},f_{\mathrm{abs}},
x_{\mathrm{rel}},x_{\mathrm{abs}})$ and \texttt{maxeval}
\Require outer tolerance \texttt{ftol\_out} and \texttt{maxit\_out}

\State Initialize $(B,M,S,\Sigma)$
\State $\rho \gets \lambda W$

\For{$h = 1,\ldots,\texttt{maxit\_out}$}

  \State $\Omega^{(h)}
    \gets \Call{GraphicalLasso}{\Sigma^{(h-1)},\rho}$
  \Comment{precision / sparsity update}

  \State $(B^{(h)},M^{(h)},S^{(h)})
    \gets
    \Call{NLOPT}{
      B^{(h-1)},M^{(h-1)},S^{(h-1)};
      \Omega^{(h)}
    }$
  \Comment{inner CCSAQ solve}

  \Statex \hspace{\algorithmicindent}
  \Comment{NLOPT stops by ftol\_rel/abs, xtol\_rel/abs or maxeval}

  \State $\Sigma^{(h)}
    \gets
    n^{-1}\left[
      {M^{(h)}}^\top M^{(h)}
      + \sum_i S_i^{(h)}
    \right]$

  \State $F_h
    \gets
    -\mathrm{ELBO}(B^{(h)},M^{(h)},S^{(h)},\Omega^{(h)})
    + \lambda\|\Omega^{(h)}\|_{1,W}$

  \If{$|F_h-F_{h-1}|/|F_h| < \texttt{ftol\_out}$}
    \State \textbf{break}
  \EndIf

\EndFor

\State \Return $(B,M,S,\Omega,\Sigma)$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
```

@algo-plnnetwork is the block-coordinate scheme of
@chiquetVariationalInferenceSparse2018: graphical lasso updates
$\boldsymbol{\Omega}$, then NLopt updates $(B,M,S)$. Inner stopping uses
`ftol_*`, `xtol_*` and `maxeval`; outer stopping uses `ftol_out` and
`maxit_out`.

#### Hyperparameters

Inside each type-time subset the call is of the form
`abundance ~ 1 + offset(log_library)`, with `log_library` the natural
log of that cell's library size. @tbl-pln-hyperparameters lists the
knobs that change either sparsity or numerical convergence.

| Control | Role | Default we use |
|---------|------|----------------|
| `penalties` (or `nPenalties`, `min.ratio`) | Sparsity path $\lambda$; larger $\lambda$ gives a sparser $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$ | Package grid, then @sec-grn-penalty-path |
| `penalty_weights` | Edge-specific weights $w_{gg'}$ in $\rho_{gg'}=\lambda w_{gg'}$ | Ones (no adaptive prior) |
| `penalize_diagonal` | Whether diagonal precision entries are penalised | `FALSE` |
| `algorithm` | Inner NLopt solver for $(B,M,S)$ | **`CCSAQ`** |
| `ftol_rel` / `ftol_abs` | Inner **objective** tolerances | `1e-8` / `0` |
| `xtol_rel` / `xtol_abs` | Inner **parameter** tolerances | `1e-4` / solver default |
| `maxeval` | Cap on one inner NLopt call | `10000` |
| `ftol_out` | Outer relative change of the penalised ELBO | `1e-5` |
| `maxit_out` | Cap on glasso $\leftrightarrow$ NLopt alternations | `50` |

: Core `PLNnetwork` hyperparameters. {#tbl-pln-hyperparameters}

`CCSAQ` is a conservative quadratic separable approximation with bound
constraints; NLopt recommends trying it before MMA. `LBFGS`, `VAR1` and
`VAR2` remain alternatives if the inner solve is the bottleneck, not
the default.

Zero-inflated PLN is not the default (@nte-drop-zico).

::: {#nte-pln-offset .callout-note}
## :information_source: The offset compares library-size-adjusted rates

In the simplest Poisson GLM for a gene $g$ and cell (or sample) $c$,

$$
Y_{gc}\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\mu_{gc}),
\qquad
\log\mu_{gc}
=
\log L_{c}
+
\beta_{0g}
+
\beta_{1g}X_{c},
$$

the term $\log L_{c}$ is an **offset**: its coefficient is fixed at
one. The mean therefore factors as
$\mu_{gc}=L_{c}\,q_{gc}$ with rate
$q_{gc}=\exp(\beta_{0g}+\beta_{1g}X_{c})$. The response remains the
**raw count**; the offset makes the condition coefficient a log ratio
of rates,

$$
\beta_{1g}
=
\log(q_{gB}/q_{gA}),
$$

not a log ratio of raw read counts. `PLNnetwork` uses the same device
in @eq-pln: $S_{c}$ (library size) multiplies the latent intensity, so
the latent Gaussian $\log\boldsymbol{Z}_{c}$ is a model for
**relative** abundance after sequencing exposure.

@fig-poisson-offset shows the two-condition cartoon. Equal rates and a
doubled library yield doubled counts but $\beta_{1}=0$. A 1.5-fold
rate increase at doubled depth yields $\beta_{1}=\ln(1.5)\approx0.405$
($\log_{2}$ fold change $\approx 0.585$).

McCarthy, Chen and Smyth write the RNA-seq GLM with the (effective)
library size as an offset in the linear predictor, so that the
condition coefficient is a log ratio of relative abundances after
sequencing depth [@mccarthyDifferentialExpressionAnalysis2012a].
DESeq2 uses the same multiplicative mean $\mu_{gc}=s_{c}q_{gc}$, with
$s_{c}$ a size factor and $q_{gc}$ the abundance that carries the fold
change [@loveModeratedEstimationFold2014]. In PLN we pass
`offset(log_library)` rather than transforming $Y$. The offset is
relative normalisation, not conversion to absolute molecule counts.

![Library-size offset in a Poisson log-link: raw counts scale with
sequencing depth, while $\beta_{1}$ is the log ratio of
library-size-adjusted expression rates.](images/poisson_offset.png){#fig-poisson-offset}
:::

### Dense shrinkage covariance, judged by held-out likelihood {#sec-shrinkage}

DeCovarT's likelihood uses $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}$, not the graph of
$\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{j}$. The bulk covariance
$\sum_{j}p_{j}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}$ of @eq-grn-convolution has
no sparse precision even when every $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{j}$ is
sparse. The fifth strategy estimates $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}$ directly
by linear shrinkage, with no penalty path and no graph
[@schäferShrinkageApproachLargescale2005]. It is the plug-in to use
when the graphical lasso returns an empty graph, because an empty graph
discards all covariance.

#### Estimator

The general form shrinks the unbiased sample covariance $S$ towards a
target $T$,
$S^{\ast}=\lambda T+(1-\lambda)S$ with $\lambda\in[0,1]$
[@schäferShrinkageApproachLargescale2005, eq. 3]. Their recommended
target D, "diagonal, unequal variance", keeps the variances and shrinks
the correlations towards zero [@schäferShrinkageApproachLargescale2005,
Table 1 and eq. 10]:

$$
s^{\ast}_{gg}=s_{gg},
\qquad
s^{\ast}_{gg'}=r^{\ast}_{gg'}\sqrt{s_{gg}s_{g'g'}},
\qquad
r^{\ast}_{gg'}=r_{gg'}\,\min\bigl(1,\max(0,1-\hat\lambda^{\ast})\bigr),
\qquad
\hat\lambda^{\ast}
=
\frac{\sum_{g\neq g'}\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(r_{gg'})}
     {\sum_{g\neq g'}r_{gg'}^{2}}.
$$ {#eq-shrink-target-d}

$\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(r_{gg'})$ is the unbiased variance of the
empirical correlation, computed on the standardised genes $z$. With
$w_{cgg'}=z_{cg}z_{cg'}$ and
$\bar w_{gg'}=n^{-1}\sum_{c}w_{cgg'}$, it is
$n(n-1)^{-3}\sum_{c}(w_{cgg'}-\bar w_{gg'})^{2}$
[@schäferShrinkageApproachLargescale2005, Appendix A]. The intensity
$\hat\lambda^{\ast}$ minimises the Frobenius risk
$\mathbb{E}\|S^{\ast}-\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\|_{F}^{2}$ in closed form,
following the Ledoit–Wolf lemma.

Properties that matter here
[@schäferShrinkageApproachLargescale2005, pp. 2–13]:

- $S^{\ast}$ is positive definite and well conditioned for any $n$ and
  $p$, including $p>n$. It is a convex combination of a positive
  definite target and a positive semidefinite $S$.
- It costs about twice the sample covariance: no penalty path, no
  cross-validation, no MCMC.
- Shrinking correlations rather than covariances makes it invariant to
  the scale of each gene, like @eq-glasso.
- The precision $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}=(S^{\ast})^{-1}$ is
  dense. Partial correlations and a local-FDR graph can be read off it
  when a network is also wanted
  [@schäferShrinkageApproachLargescale2005, eqs. 11–15].

`corpcor::cov.shrink()` implements it [@R-corpcor]. Version 1.6.10
also shrinks the variances towards their median by default
(`lambda.var` estimated). Pass `lambda.var = 0` to reproduce target D
exactly. `corpcor` is not yet in `renv.lock`: run
`renv::install("corpcor")`, then `renv::snapshot()`, before the
pipeline uses it.

#### Held-out Gaussian likelihood as the arbiter

$\hat\lambda^{\ast}$ is optimal for Frobenius risk, not for the Gaussian
likelihood that DeCovarT evaluates. We therefore compare covariance
estimates by **held-out** log-likelihood. The paper does not do this; it
is our addition. Chiquet recommends $K$-fold cross-validation when the
target is prediction rather than the true model
[@chiquetContributionsSparseMethods2015, p. 78].

For type $j$ at time $t$, split the cells into $K$ folds. Fit
$(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{(-k)},\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{(-k)})$
on the other folds, and score the $n_k$ held-out cells by

$$
\ell^{(k)}
=
-\frac{1}{2}\Bigl[
\log\det\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{(-k)}
+
\operatorname{tr}\bigl\{(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{(-k)})^{-1}S_{k}\bigr\}
+
p\log 2\pi
\Bigr],
$$ {#eq-heldout-loglik}

where $S_{k}=n_k^{-1}\sum_{c\in k}(x_{c}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{(-k)})(x_{c}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{(-k)})^{\top}$.
Average $\ell^{(k)}$ over folds and compare four estimates of
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}$:

1. the diagonal of marginal variances (the "empty graph");
2. the shrinkage estimate at $\hat\lambda^{\ast}$, and on a grid of
   $\lambda$ as a sensitivity check of the closed-form intensity;
3. the `glasso` covariance at the EBIC $\lambda$, refit on its support;
4. the `PLNnetwork` latent covariance, mapped to the scale of $x$.

The folds split cells of **one** specimen, so the score measures
generalisation to new cells of that gastruloid, not to new specimens
(@sec-grn-scope).

```{r}
#| label: shrinkage-heldout-sketch
#| eval: false
# Sketch: dense shrinkage covariance per type and held-out likelihood.
# x: cells x genes, log1p counts of one type at one time.
heldout_loglik <- function(sigma, mu, x_test) {
  centred <- sweep(x_test, 2L, mu)
  s_test <- crossprod(centred) / nrow(x_test)
  ld <- as.numeric(determinant(sigma, logarithm = TRUE)$modulus)
  -0.5 * (ld + sum(diag(solve(sigma, s_test))) + ncol(x_test) * log(2 * pi))
}

fold <- withr::with_seed(1L, sample(rep_len(1:5, nrow(x))))
scores <- vapply(1:5, function(k) {
  train <- x[fold != k, , drop = FALSE]
  test <- x[fold == k, , drop = FALSE]
  mu <- colMeans(train)
  shrunk <- corpcor::cov.shrink(train, lambda.var = 0, verbose = FALSE)
  diagonal <- diag(apply(train, 2L, stats::var))
  c(
    shrinkage = heldout_loglik(unclass(shrunk), mu, test),
    diagonal = heldout_loglik(diagonal, mu, test)
  )
}, numeric(2))
rowMeans(scores)
```

## Choosing the penalty {#sec-grn-penalty-path}

Four displays, and only these, are used to pick the penalty for each of
the three estimators. Partial-correlation **weights** matter, so heatmaps
show the precision, not a binary adjacency.

### Stability criteria {#sec-grn-penalty-stability}

These plots decide $\lambda$ (`huge`), $\alpha$ (`SILGGM`; we use
$0.05$), or the PLN penalty grid. They are **not** the final
cell-type report.

1. **Regularisation paths.** Plot each off-diagonal entry of
   $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}(\lambda)$ against $\lambda$ or
   $\log\lambda$. This is the classical lasso path: which edges enter
   as the penalty relaxes. The figures keep five edges that survive at
   $\lambda^{\star}$ and five that are driven to zero.
2. **EBIC against $\lambda$.** Plot $\mathrm{EBIC}_{\gamma}(\lambda)$
   against $\log\lambda$, with a rug of evaluated penalties and a mark
   at the minimiser [@foygelExtendedBayesianInformation2010]. Overlay
   $\gamma\in\{0,0.25,0.5\}$ when that hyperparameter is free. A flat
   valley means many penalties are equivalent.
3. **Edge density against EBIC.** Put the undirected density
   $|E|/\bigl(G(G-1)/2\bigr)$ on the horizontal axis and EBIC on the
   vertical axis, and mark the optimum. That is the sparsity–fit
   tradeoff without depending on the numerical scale of $\lambda$.
4. **Weighted interval score.** For consecutive penalties, combine EBIC
   curvature, the change in support, and the Frobenius gap of
   $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$. Large scores are the intervals the
   adaptive search bisects.

StARS is not one of these four displays (@nte-stars-cost).

For `SILGGM`, repeat the same pictures with the FDR level in place of
$\lambda$ when a path of $\alpha$ is computed. For `PLNnetwork`, the
horizontal axis is the sparsity penalty grid.

### Descriptive plots per cell type {#sec-grn-penalty-describe}

Once a penalty is fixed, two figure folders (not a single mixed
gallery) report the selected networks.

**Folder 1 — one type, one time, all estimators.** A `funkyheatmap`
table with rows = cell types (or type $\times$ time) and columns =
global scores of each selected network: EBIC, Hellinger distance to
the empirical cell cloud, mean off-diagonal edge density, number of
edges, and a degree-distribution summary (mean degree; a bar plot of
degrees sits beside the heatmap, never as a transcriptome hairball).
Partial-correlation heatmaps at the selected penalty use a **frozen**
gene order (cluster once) and

$$
\rho_{gg'\mid\mathrm{rest}}
=
-\frac{\omega_{gg'}}{\sqrt{\omega_{gg}\omega_{g'g'}}}.
$$ {#eq-partial}

Blocks that survive a stronger penalty are the stable ones.

**Folder 2 — pairwise type comparisons.** The same global scores, now
as pairwise contrasts (difference or ratio of EBIC, Hellinger,
density, \ldots) between cell types at a fixed time. This is the rewiring view at the **metric** level;
signed partial-correlation difference heatmaps belong with the
visualisations in @sec-metrics-viz.

## Core estimators {#sec-grn-top4}

This chapter's product is the **three** sparse precision estimators,
not the full $3\times 2\times 2$ design of @fig-pipeline (lifts and
gene panels are later chapters). The `ppcor` baseline (@sec-ppcor) and
the dense shrinkage covariance (@sec-shrinkage) are reference points.
The first checks the penalties; the second is the DeCovarT plug-in
when no graph is needed.

$$
\{\texttt{glasso},\;
\texttt{SILGGM+NPN},\;
\texttt{PLNnetwork}\}.
$$ {#eq-grn-product}

Every core method must finally export

$$
\bigl\{
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j},\,
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j},\,
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{j}
\bigr\}_{j=1}^{J},
\qquad
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{j}
=
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}^{-1}
\succ 0,
$$ {#eq-grn-export}

on the linear scale of @eq-grn-convolution, not on NPN scores.

| Estimator | Reference | What it estimates | Pros | Cons |
|-----------|-----------|-------------------|------|------|
| `glasso` | @friedmanSparseInverseCovariance2008; @R-glasso | Sparse Gaussian $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$ | Fast; unpenalised diagonal; EBIC path | Needs Gaussian rows; no library-size layer |
| `SILGGM` `D-S_GL` | @zhangSILGGMExtensivePackage2018; @liuGaussianGraphicalModel2013 | De-sparsified edges, then an FDR support | Global FDR at $\alpha=0.05$; large $n$ makes modes agree | $\check{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$ is dense; NPN changes the mean |
| `PLNnetwork` | @chiquetPoissonLognormalModelVersatile2021 | Latent precision of a PLN | Counts and offset; variational, not MCMC | Heavier than graphical lasso; no edgewise FDR |

: Three core precision estimators. {#tbl-grn-core}

The knobs that @sec-grn-penalty-path is meant to set are $\lambda$
(`glasso`), $\alpha=0.05$ (`SILGGM`), and the PLN penalty grid.

::: {#nte-drop-zico .callout-warning}
## :warning: Why we drop zero-inflated directed graphs in the core

Directed zero-inflated DAGs are the wrong object for DeCovarT: the
output is a DAG, not an undirected SPD precision. Suppinger is droplet
UMI data. Svensson showed that zeros in droplet scRNA-seq are often
explained by ordinary molecule-sampling counts
[@svenssonDropletScRNAseqNot2020]. Keep hurdle or ZINB graphs in
@sec-sensitivity if the observation model is to be contaminated, not as
a GRN estimator.
:::

## Perspectives {#sec-grn-appendix}

### Cartesian `GmGM` cannot separate within-cell edges {#sec-gmgm}

`GmGM` replaces independent cells by a Cartesian product: gene $g$ in
cell $c$ may depend on other genes in the same cell, or on the same
gene in other cells, but not on an arbitrary pair $(c,g)\neq(c',g')$
[@andrewMakingMultiaxisGaussian2026]. The precision of the vectorised
matrix is a Kronecker **sum** of a gene precision and a cell precision.
That sum forbids the cross terms that would distinguish regulation
inside a cell from dependence across cells.

A strong-product Gaussian graphical model is the extension that can
carry both within-cell and across-cell edges. It is not available as a
drop-in for this design. @fig-gmgm-extend sketches why labelled types
still do not rescue the Cartesian support: hard cell-type blocks remove
cross-type edges, but inside a type the Cartesian sum still cannot
separate intracellular regulation from cell–cell dependence.

![Cartesian GmGM, type-specific fits, and the strong-product extension
that would separate within-cell edges from across-cell
edges.](images/gmgm_complexity.png){#fig-gmgm-extend}

### Sparse plus low-rank precisions {#sec-lowrank}

Unmeasured programmes can make the marginal precision dense.
Chandrasekaran, Parrilo and Willsky split it into a sparse conditional
graph minus a low-rank factor term
[@chandrasekaranLatentVariableGraphical2012],

$$
\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\mathrm{marg}}
=
\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\mathrm{sparse}}
-
\boldsymbol{L},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{L}\succeq 0.
$$ {#eq-slr}

A useful reading of $\boldsymbol{L}$ is a small set of transcription
factors, or of co-regulated pathways, that lower the rank of the
residual dependence. $\boldsymbol{L}$ is a nuisance for DeCovarT, not a
type covariance. This check is not in the $3\times 2\times 2$ product.

### Fused graphical lasso on a PLN

Related types can share part of a graph. The joint graphical lasso
[@danaherJointGraphicalLasso2012] penalises both sparsity and the gap
between $\omega_{gg'}^{(j)}$ and $\omega_{gg'}^{(\ell)}$. PLNFGL puts a
Poisson-lognormal sampling layer under that fused penalty
[@zhaiPLNFGLJointEstimation2026]. Fusion can shrink away the rewiring
DeCovarT is meant to keep, so it stays out of the independent-type
comparison.

### Other copula joints

JGCGM learns shared and subgroup-specific edges under a Gaussian copula
and warns against a naive nonparanormal map on counts
[@wuJointLearningMultiple2020]. It does not replace `PLNnetwork` on UMI
counts. Structured penalties from earlier Chiquet work
[@chiquetSparsitySigncoherentGroups2012] could encode pathway modules;
they are optional regularisers, not a fourth core estimator.
